name: Ikizu
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Aunio, Lotta, Holly Robinson, Tim Roth, Oliver Stegen & John B. Walker. 2019. The Mara languages (JE40). In Mark Van de Velde, Koen Bostoen, Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 2nd edn, 501-532. London: Routledge. [accepted manuscript, Helda handle 10138/322322; main text and separate tables file]
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure', accepted-manuscript p. 7; nominal-tone paragraphs, pp. 9-10, with Table 7 'Ikizu nominal tones' in the separate tables file (tables p. 8); Infinitive tone, p. 12 with ex. (22). Print pp. 501-532; exact print page not seen.
catalog_quote: The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme with the exception of Kabwa double H pattern (see below). ... Ikizu also assigns tones to moras but counts syllables. ... None of the languages have underlying contrasts between level H and contour tones, except Ikizu in some restricted contexts. ... In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult, and in Ikizu, the lexical tone spread does not target the utterance-final syllable. ... Tone spread is attested in Ikizu, Kabwa, and Simbiti. In Ikizu, for example, the penultimate and antepenultimate lexical Hs spread right to the rest of the nominal stem (see Table 7 below). ... Ikizu has two tonal patterns for monosyllabic noun stems and three patterns for longer stems (Table 7), with H spreading to the end of the stem. ... in Ikizu the three underlying patterns are ØØØ, HØØ, and ØHØ. However, Ikizu toneless patterns are realised with a stem-initial H when the noun is pronounced in isolation. ... As with nouns, Ikizu assigns the Infinitive H in relation to the end of the stem: the H is assigned to the antepenultimate syllable of the macrostem. When the macrostem has fewer than three syllables, the Infinitive H is realised macrostem-initially.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Routledge, pp. 501-532'). Every sentence of the quote is present verbatim (line breaks only): 'The underlying contrast is between H and Ø (toneless) since only H tones are active in the tonal rules. There is at most one lexical H tone per morpheme' and 'Ikizu also assigns tones to moras but counts syllables' and 'In Simbiti and Ikizu, melodic Hs are shifted from the utterance-final syllable to the penult, and in Ikizu, the lexical tone spread does not target the utterance-final syllable' are on draft p. 7 (sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ikizu is described as a privative-H tone language, not a stress language: noun stems are lexically toneless, penult-H or antepenult-H (Table 7: ùmù-ɾìmì 'farmer' / òmò-ɾámú 'brother-in-law' / ùmú-βísá 'enemy'), with the H spreading rightward to the end of the stem except onto an utterance-final syllable; toneless nouns get a stem-initial H in isolation; the Infinitive H sits on the antepenult of the macrostem. No source opened makes any statement about word stress in Ikizu; the chapter's only 'penultimate stress' remark concerns Zanaki.
new_statements.exceptions: Ikizu allows contour tones 'in some restricted contexts'; the toneless/H contrast of nouns is neutralised in isolation (stem-initial H inserted). Orthography Statement p. 9 adds that phonemic long vowels in noun stems occur almost exclusively in the penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Nominal tone is stated for the stem and for phrase-medial vs utterance-final (isolation) forms; verb melodies are stated for the macrostem. No word-stress domain is discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ikizu proper (JE402, [ikz]) as spoken in Bunda/Musoma districts; the SIL orthography covers Ikizu-Sizaki jointly (Sizaki [szk] was merged into ikz by ISO change request 2007-033). The Mara chapter's Ikizu data are the same SIL/Helsinki corpus used by Aunio & Robinson.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Tone and syllable structure' (draft p. 7): Mara languages contrast H vs toneless; Ikizu assigns tones to moras but counts syllables; utterance-final melodic H shifts to the penult and lexical H spread does not target the utterance-final syllable. Nominal tone (draft p. 9, Table 7): Ikizu nouns have three underlying patterns ØØØ / HØØ / ØHØ, i.e. toneless, penult H, antepenult H, with H spreading to the end of the stem; toneless nouns surface with a stem-initial H in isolation. Verbal tone (draft p. 12): Infinitive H on the antepenult of the macrostem. 'Penultimate stress' is stated…

sources.citation: Robinson, Holly (author). 2016. Ikizu-Sizaki Orthography Statement, Approved Orthography Edition, April 2016. SIL International, Uganda-Tanzania Branch. 64 pp. (updated version of Gray & Smith 2010 Ikizu Orthography Sketch)
sources.note: Sec. 2.3 Tone, p. 19: 'Ikizu has lexical tone on nouns, but this tone does not have a high functional load and therefore is not written in the orthography.. Ikizu also has a variety of grammatical tone melodies, but none of them are contrastive.' Sec. 2.1.2, p. 9: in noun stems phonemic long vowels occur 'almost exclusively in the penultimate syllable'. No stress or accent statement.

sources.citation: Aunio, Lotta. 2015. A typological perspective on Bantu nominal tone: the case of Ikoma-Nata-Isenye in western Tanzania. Southern African Linguistics and Applied Language Studies 33(3): 359-371. doi:10.2989/16073614.2015.1105106 [Helda accepted manuscript]
sources.note: Draft p. 12 (print c. p. 368), one paragraph on Ikizu: aligns nominal lexical tones to the right edge of the stem; nouns are toneless (umu-ɾimi 'farmer') or have penult H (omo-ɾámu) or antepenult H (umú-βisa); systematic rightward H spread except utterance-finally; toneless utterances not allowed, so toneless nouns get an antepenultimate or stem-initial H in isolation; phrase-medially [-Oblig(H)] [-Culm(H)]. No stress statement.

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog narr1281). Surveys Bantu nominal tone systems, dividing them into mora/syllable-assigning systems (tone contrastive on every stem mora/syllable, or with restrictions) and stem-assigning demarcative systems (tones assigned relative to stem/word edges, same number of patterns for all stem lengths), and argues the stress-like and tone-like properties do not form an implicational hierarchy; Ikizu-specific content unverified.
sources.venue: The Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages
